items.title: Ask Ethan: Can you explain the Higgs boson in depth?
items.summary: One of the great quests in all of science is to discover, at a fundamental level, what the Universe is actually made of. If you took every amount of matter and energy that existed — or even could exist — and cut it up into its smallest possible chunks, until only something that was uncuttable was left, you’d be left with the fundamental, elementary particles that composed our Universe. In physics, this took us first down to the level of the atom, then to atomic nuclei and electrons, then to protons, neutrons, and electrons, and finally to our modern Standard Model of elementary particles: complete with quarks, charged leptons, neutrinos, their antimatter counterparts, the gluons, the photon, the W-and-Z bosons, and one additional unique particle, the Higgs boson. Of all of those particles, the Higgs boson is the most recently discovered particle: found only at particle accelerators, like the Large Hadron Collider at CERN, in 2012. But what’s the story of the Higgs boson? What makes it so unique, where does it come from, and how does it fit in with everything else that we know? That’s what Vu H Nguyen wants to know, asking: “Can you explain the Higgs boson in depth? [It is] difficult for me to understand, but I think this is very important in particle physics. Maybe you can explain it in an easier way?” When we think about matter, we normally think about “fundamental” in the way we outlined above: by cutting it up into its smallest indivisible component parts. But there’s more to the story, and the Higgs boson requires us to go deeper than any other known particle in order to understand it. Here’s the story. From macroscopic scales down to subatomic ones, the sizes of the fundamental particles play only a small role in determining the sizes of composite structures. Whether the building blocks are truly fundamental and/or point-like particles is still not known, but we do understand the Universe from large, cosmic scales down to tiny, subatomic ones. The scale of electrons, quarks, and gluons is the limit to how far we’ve ever probed nature: down to scales of ~10^-19 meters, where these structures remain point-like. Credit : Magdalena Kowalska/CERN/ISOLDE team Here in our Universe, we’re mostly familiar with the particles that are common and stable today: atoms and the subatomic particles they’re composed of. Atoms are made of electrons that orbit the atomic nucleus, which in turn is made of protons and neutrons, which themselves are made of quarks and gluons. If you want to see what types of quarks are in there, however, you have to collide particles together. You have to collide them hard enough to break inside the atom, to crack open the atomic nucleus, to split apart the individual protons and neutrons, and to smash them directly into individual elementary particles. When you do that, you discover something amazing. You don’t just reveal what these composite structures inside the atom are made of; you also gain the ability to create brand new particles, including heavy, unstable, short-lived particles. Through the power of colliders, we don’t just make electrons and the up-and-down quarks that compose protons and neutrons, but also: muons and taus, the heavier cousins of electrons, positrons, antimuons, and antitaus, the antimatter counterparts of those charged leptons, strange, charm, bottom, and top quarks, the antimatter counterparts of all six flavors of quarks (the antiquarks), photons, gluons, and W-and-Z bosons, which are the gauge bosons, and the Higgs boson as well. These, along with the neutrinos and antineutrinos (which can’t be directly observed in colliders, but can be observed through other means), make up all of the known elementary particles, and the entirety of the Standard Model of elementary particles. This diagram of the Standard Model particles shows the fermions in the top row, the gauge bosons in the middle row, and the Higgs on the bottom. The lines indicate couplings, and you can see which fermionic particles couple to which of the forces by the blue lines. Everything with mass couples to the Higgs; the only particles which are massless (and hence, do not) are the photon and the gluons. The theoretical graviton, not shown here, couples to everything with energy: all particles and antiparticles. If there are new particles out there, their couplings may reveal their presence, indirectly, through precision measurements that compare the particles’ observed properties with those predicted by the Standard Model. Credit : TriTertButoxy/Stannered at English Wikipedia We can measure all sorts of properties about these particles from our collider-detector experiments. In particular, we can, by creating enough of them and building detectors around the collision points where those particles come into existence — created from energy via Einstein’s E = mc as long as all of the necessary quantum properties like energy, momentum, angular momentum, electric charge, and so on are conserved — measure all sorts of properties associated with them. We can determine: their rest masses, their electric charges, their intrinsic angular momenta (i.e., their spin), their mean lifetimes, their weak hypercharge and weak isospin, their possible decay products (all of the different pathways through which the unstable ones can decay), and their branching ratios (the rate at which they decay through their various pathways), chief among them. The Standard Model isn’t just about the particles that exist, but about their key relationships and properties. The quarks and leptons make up what we conventionally know of as “matter” (while the antiquarks and antileptons make up “antimatter”), but the gauge bosons determine how they interact with one another. We normally talk about this as the four fundamental forces, as particles and antiparticles interact through gravity (which we don’t know whether it’s quantum in nature; it’s outside of the Standard Model), electromagnetism (mediated by the photon), the weak nuclear force (mediated by the W-and-Z bosons), and the strong nuclear force (mediated by the gluons). Sure, there are still mysteries that we have that the Standard Model can’t explain: gravity, the values for the rest masses of the particles, the abundance of matter over antimatter in the Universe, and the existence of dark matter and dark energy among them. But for what the Standard Model does give us, it’s an incredibly powerful description of reality. The rest masses of the fundamental particles in the Universe determine when and under what conditions they can be created, and also relate to how long they can survive after their creation during the hot Big Bang. The more massive a particle is, the less time it can spontaneously be created in the early Universe, and the shorter its lifetime will be. Although we can explain particle masses through a coupling to the Higgs, we have no way of successfully predicting their values; they must be experimentally measured in order to be determined. Credit : Universe-review So where does the Higgs boson come from? In order to answer that, we can’t start here in our Universe today, nor can we even start with the “little bangs” we create in our particle colliders here on Earth. Instead, we have to go all the way back to the hot Big Bang, where higher energies and hotter temperatures were achieved than in anything we can create here on Earth. Back then, we still had the quarks and leptons (and antiquarks and antileptons) that we have today, as well as the gluons. They all still needed energy in order to exist, but they didn’t possess the rest masses that they have today. items.title: Life is the most important problem in physics
items.summary: Descartes cut open living dogs and insisted their cries were just the noises of a machine. Astrophysicist and astrobiologist Adam Frank, a professor at the University of Rochester and author of The Little Book of Aliens, argues that the same life-as-machine metaphor still shapes how we think about AI, and that it gets life fundamentally wrong. Living things are self-creating, self-repairing systems that decide what matters to them, which is why he calls today’s AI an artificial mimic rather than an intelligence. This video Life is the most important problem in physics is featured on Big Think .

items.title: A medieval map mystery may finally be solved
items.summary: “We’ll just have to think our way back, step by step.” That’s what the Dutch geodesist Roelof Nicolai said in 2014 in a Strange Maps article . Nicolai had just spent his PhD years discovering that portolan charts — those gorgeous, wind-rose-covered coastline maps that suddenly appeared in Mediterranean ports in the second half of the 13th century — were geometrically too accurate to have been made the way everyone assumed. Something else was going on. Twelve years on, we might have an answer. Tome Marelić, an assistant professor of geography at the University of Zadar in Croatia (and the current vice chair of the Working Group on the History of Cartography within the International Cartographic Association), has spent years doing exactly the step-by-step thinking Nicolai prescribed in 2014. Read together, his scientific articles amount to the most detailed forensic examination portolan charts have ever received. And the story they tell is more satisfying than even the more out-there theories (including “aliens did it”). Mapping the Mediterranean Dated to the latter part of the 13th century, the anonymous Carte Pisane is the oldest surviving portolan chart. However, its high degree of accuracy suggests that it is not the beginning, but the continuation of a long tradition. So where did that knowledge come from? (Credit: Tome Marelić: Classical antiquity origin of spatial data underlying portolan charts: how Pietro Vesconte might have assembled the Carta Riccardiana utilising maps in Marinus of Tyre’s projection, 2026) First, a quick refresher. A portolan chart is a nautical chart of the Mediterranean, western European, and northwest African coasts, criss-crossed with dense color-coded web-like networks often called “rhumb lines,” dotted with harbor names written perpendicular to the coast (so you had to keep spinning the chart to read it). The charts are calibrated with little beaded scale bars marking off distances in miglia , or so-called portolan miles whose roots remained enigmatic for decades until Marelić’s recently proposed explanation. (A Portolan mile is a bit shorter than a modern statute mile.) The oldest surviving example, the anonymous Carte Pisane , appeared in Italy around 1270. Geometrically speaking, it looks like a finished product. There’s no awkward teenage phase of European cartography preceding it — no 13th-century equivalent of a flip phone before the smartphone. It just arrives, fully formed, with Mediterranean coastlines accurate enough to almost look like a map from today. “The immense accuracy of coastline renderings on portolan charts, which, as far as is known, suddenly appeared in mid- to late-13th century, was never fully and objectively explained,” says Marelić. Romantic and seemingly plausible — but wrong The traditional explanation is romantic and, at first glance, plausible: Generations of sailors recorded their compass bearings and estimated distances in logbooks, and cartographers eventually compiled all that dead-reckoning data into a single chart. The trouble, as Nicolai discovered first , is that the numbers don’t work. Simulate a medieval ship captain’s best-effort compass-and-guesswork navigation, average enough of those readings together, and you get a chart ten times less accurate than the actual portolan chart. This is where Marelić comes in. His method of choice is cartometric analysis — precise, computer-assisted measurements and error-computations. Take an old chart, digitize it, pin a few hundred identifiable points (ports, capes, river mouths, islands) to their true modern coordinates, and let the software calculate exactly how much the old map agrees with the modern map in a certain projection by scaling and rotating it until their geometrical best fit is obtained. The size of that remaining mismatch, expressed in measurable distance, tells you how accurate the chart really is, and even the exact magnitude and direction of errors for every pinned point. Random surveying errors should scatter every which way. Systemic errors, however, typically point to the map projection fabric in the background, which is sometimes, and especially in this case, invisible to the naked eye. Marelić meticulously scrutinized that background fabric for years, stumbling upon some groundbreaking and intricate findings along the way. Finding #1: Mosaics that defy the medieval origin narrative Marelić confirmed and quantified that when you cut a portolan chart into regional bits — Western Mediterranean, Adriatic, Aegean, and so on — and georeference each bit separately, the accuracy roughly doubles compared to the map as a whole. That is what you’d expect if a cartographer had glued together several pre-existing charts of slightly different appearances into one seamless-looking whole. Considered separately, the parts of a portolan chart are more accurate than the whole – which is what you’d expect if a mapmaker had glued together several pre-existing charts. (Credit: Tome Marelić: Cartometric Analyses: Methodological Issues and Their Significance for the History of Cartography and Historical Studies in General, 2025) Although portolan chart subsections , as he dubbed them, were detected by a few earlier scholars, Marelić originally computed that the earliest known pieces — such as the anonymous Pisane, Cortona, Lucca , and Avignon charts that are often treated as somewhat primitive — have portions of coastline that are nearly identical to those on allegedly more mature charts made by Genoese cartographer Pietro Vesconte in the early 14th century. Even more intriguingly, his second article reveals that Vesconte’s charts remained the most accurate on a subsectional level for at least the next three centuries, while the third paper demonstrates that multi-sheet portolan atlases show the same pattern: images of seas that are geometrically frozen in time. Only this time, the atlases are mosaics within mosaics, with their subsections cut and sliced and arbitrarily encapsulated into sheets of varying map scales and coverages. Tellingly, none of those authors seem to have fully understood the geometry of their own work, not even those who made portolan atlases, books that allow for more liberties to depict smaller regions than one-piece charts. Compare an atlas sheet to a portolan chart made by the very same cartographer, and even they don’t quite agree. These were not confident creators; they were copyists, doing their careful but imperfect best with material they didn’t fully understand. Finding #2: The compass has an alibi One of the more curious aspects of portolan charts is that their coastlines are all tilted roughly -10° off true north. The leading explanation has always been magnetic declination: Medieval sailors trusted their compasses, not realizing that magnetic north and true north aren’t quite the same thing — thus unknowingly infusing that error into every portolan chart. It’s a neat story, but as Marelić found, it doesn’t hold water. He checked the theory against a paleomagnetic model of how Earth’s magnetic field actually behaved in the Mediterranean region between the late 13th and late 16th centuries. And the cartographic tilt doesn’t track with the magnetic reality of that era — not in degree, not in geography, not over time. Whatever initially rotated these coastlines, it wasn’t a 13th-century compass needle. In fact, his findings point to a completely different root cause: a late medieval graphical compromise between two map projections with significantly different appearances, both of which were developed about a millennium and a half before and long forgotten, but more on that later. items.title: The first DNA crime test didn’t catch the killer. It freed an innocent man.
items.summary: The events leading to the first forensic DNA case began in 1983. Lynda Mann was only 15 years old when, returning home from babysitting one evening in the Leicestershire village of Narborough, she was raped and murdered as she took a shortcut along a footpath known by villagers as the Black Pad. It was a path that would be unlikely to be known by anyone who wasn’t local, suggesting the killer was someone from the area. At the time, the biological side of forensic science was still in its infancy, though there were a handful of tests that could help narrow things down in terms of identifying the perpetrator. Investigators could determine from a semen sample that he was blood group A, which is the case for about 40% of the English population. Having established his blood group, they were able to tell that he was a “secretor,” which is true for about 70% of the population. Phosphoglucomutase (PGM) enzyme testing was also carried out. PGM is an enzyme that both men and women carry, and it comes in a number of different forms; hence, determining which type the perpetrator had could also help narrow things down. The perpetrator was found to be type PGM1+, alongside around 40% of people with European ancestry living in England. As this combination of factors would be found in around 10% of all men, it was clearly not enough to identify the killer, though it would prove to be useful information a few years later. But for the time being, despite a huge police investigation, including door-to-door inquiries in Narborough and the nearby villages of Enderby and Littlethorpe, the trail eventually went cold. Then, in 1986, another young girl, Dawn Ashworth, was also raped and murdered just off another footpath, Ten Pound Lane, this time in Enderby, very close to Narborough. As in Lynda’s case, the killer’s modus operandi pointed to someone with local knowledge of the area: both the crimes took place in a part of each village that only locals were likely to know about. The similarities in both cases led the police to link the two crimes. There was a serial killer on the loose. Then came the first twist in the story, and with it, the first time that DNA “fingerprinting” would be used in a forensic case. Richard Buckland, a kitchen porter, aged 17 at the time and with learning difficulties, had been seen in the area on a motorbike, similar to the one that had been seen in the area when Dawn went missing. He also seemed to know, even before the police did, where Dawn might be found. The police brought him in and, under questioning, Richard confessed to Dawn’s murder, but he staunchly protested his innocence when it came to the second murder: He had not killed Lynda. With Richard in custody, the police were in a quandary. They were pretty convinced they had their suspect for both cases, but they needed new evidence to break the deadlock and also connect Richard to Lynda’s murder. The detective chief superintendent of the Leicestershire Police at the time, David Baker, had read an article in the local newspaper, the Leicester Mercury, about the work of [geneticist and DNA “fingerprinting” pioneer] Alec Jeffreys in the Sarbah case [of matching a mother and son’s DNA]. David had a brainwave. The police are always looking for new ways to help solve cases, and he recognized that this new technique could be used forensically: DNA fingerprinting could take this broad biological categorization of the perpetrator from being from a group of about 10% of the population, right down to “a group of one.” And if it could do that, it would confirm whether Richard Buckland had killed both girls, and he would go to jail for his crimes. In the meantime, Alec and his team were fine-tuning the DNA fingerprinting process. While the patterns of blobs and lines generated in the first version of DNA fingerprinting were ideal for telling individuals apart from one another, they were extremely complicated and difficult to explain in court. Alec’s team had been homing in on just some of these genetic stutters to understand more about them. They had been finding more and more of them across the genome, each following the same pattern — a DNA “word” repeated over and over again many times. It wasn’t the same word as before, however, but lots of different words, each of them tandemly repeated over and over again, and some were highly variable. There tends to be a standard range of repeats that you find in a population — say, between 10 and 27. So far from seeing only three possible combinations, the number of possible combinations was in the many hundreds for one marker alone. The team homed in on markers with considerable variation in the number of repeats an individual might have, making them perfect candidates for developing a more convenient test for casework. Concentrating on these markers, fine-tuning and polishing the technique, was starting to give what the forensic community, and courts, would want: something that was quick to carry out, easy to interpret (important when explaining things to a jury) but still highly specific in terms of telling individuals apart. It became known as DNA profiling. Alongside this, Alec had published a paper showing that DNA could be extracted not only from bloodstains up to four years old, but also from semen stains. In another breakthrough, it was now possible to separate sperm cells from vaginal cells and extract DNA from them; hence, DNA fingerprinting could be used to identify the perpetrator in a rape case. Each incremental scientific discovery was slowly leading towards the much-needed breakthrough in the hunt for Dawn and Lynda’s killer. Just as there was progress on the scientific front, so there was in the police investigation. Like Alec, David Baker could see the potential of linking DNA with forensics, and he was about to give Alec his first case. Between them, they would make history not once, but twice. DNA fingerprinting could take this broad biological categorization of the perpetrator from being from a group of about 10% of the population, right down to ‘a group of one.’ David’s request was simple. Convinced that there would be a DNA match, he asked Alec if he would run a DNA fingerprinting test on Richard Buckland and then on the samples taken from Lynda. A DNA match linking Richard to Lynda would provide the evidence linking him to her murder as well — both cases would be solved in one fell swoop. Alec agreed to run the test, and samples from Lynda and Richard Buckland were transferred to his lab just weeks later. This was to be his first ever forensic case and Alec was fully aware of the importance of what he was doing. Within a few days, he knew the DNA testing had worked, and he had his results. It was time to ring David with the news — both good and bad. The good news was that the DNA analysis had worked, but the bad news was that Richard Buckland’s DNA had not been found with Lynda’s. Lynda’s killer and Richard had completely different DNA fingerprints: The police had identified the wrong suspect for that murder. David then asked Alec to repeat the process with samples from Dawn. Again, the news was both good and bad: The DNA testing was successful, but it showed that, despite Richard’s confession, he hadn’t killed Dawn either. The young lad in custody was completely innocent of the crimes he was thought to have committed. On November 21, 1986, three years to the day since Lynda had been murdered, Richard Buckland was duly released. Thus the first time that DNA fingerprinting was used in a criminal case, rather than establishing the suspect’s guilt, as anticipated, it proved their innocence and exonerated them of a crime. Without it, Richard would have been wrongly imprisoned for a double murder, almost certainly spending decades in prison for crimes he hadn’t committed.* And while Richard Buckland was the first, he certainly hasn’t been the last in all the years since then. items.title: I Need to Know How I Forgot I Wanted to Die
items.summary: What I Lost, What I Lose by Erica Dawson At my third ECT procedure, Tamara, a nurse, brought me warm blankets thin as sheets and inserted the catheter in my vein. She pushed Zofran for nausea, Toradol for pain, placed the scopolamine patch, for motion sickness, behind my left ear. The nurse anesthetist pushed a dose of caffeine equaling roughly eight cups of coffee in a few swallows. Caffeine lengthens the duration of the grand mal seizure, which is therapeutically beneficial, apparently, in combating treatment-resistant bipolar depression. So far, I wasn’t seizing long enough. I hadn’t had caffeine in months, for fear of it triggering mania. Here, in the hospital, the stimulant hit my blood and I started trembling so hard I got confused, in sheer panic, and thought they held the electrodes to my head, inducing the seizure while I was still awake. My heart rate increased and as the beeping from the pulse monitor became more and more urgent, I became convinced I was in cardiac arrest, about to flat line, and I wasn’t mad at that. They laid the gurney all the way down. Someone pressed on my shoulders, trying to minimize the shaking. I heard the doctor’s voice. Somebody said propofol . I woke up in the recovery room, disappointed, alive, still suicidal with a plan and intent, my voice cracking as I spoke to the nurse, asking for apple juice. Since having electroconvulsive therapy, I can’t remember parts of the past and, often, can’t make new memories. While I remember some moments from the hospital like this, I played the piano my whole life and now can’t read music. I studied Shakespeare to get a PhD and, the other day, had to look up the name of the guy who tricked Othello into murdering Desdemona. I can’t read long form writing; I can’t remember what happened in the previous pages. I don’t watch TV shows with several characters or complicated plots that play out over more than one episode. I spend a lot of time trying to goad my brain into recalling things I’ve lost and continued to lose on a daily basis. I look at photographs in my phone, ask people repetitive questions. I go down this road because, with a brain that oscillates between two extreme moods, I need the kind of stasis that comes from knowing where you’ve been or what you’ve done or what you can do. The exquisite hippocampus at its best. I can revisit having my head in Mom’s lap after ECT as she tried to massage the headaches out. I can remember rubbing my calves; it felt as if all 600 plus of my muscles hurt. I can go way back and tread through the grass of our old backyard, wrap my small hand around the swing set’s pole, lean back, and twirl. But out of 46 years of memories, what I need to know most is exactly how and when, during ECT, I stopped remembering I wanted to die. I’m not sure when I began considering ECT as an option to treat my bipolar depression. My doctor labeled me treatment-resistant a long time before. I tried all the meds. Mood stabilizers. Anticonvulsants. Antipsychotics. I underwent transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). Nothing helped with the suicidality. I attended two partial hospitalization programs where, essentially, you’re admitted during the day for intensive care, support groups, and medication management, but allowed to go home at night. Every evening before I left the first program, in the exit assessment, a nurse would ask me if I had thoughts of harming myself. Each time, I answered yes . Placing the problems with the US healthcare system aside, I usually had the safety net of my mom at home. She flew from Maryland to Florida frequently, often for weeks at a time. She removed all sharp objects from the apartment, hid my medication, doling out only a single day’s pills. When she wasn’t in town, we’d FaceTime 24 hours straight and my medicine was kept at my best friend’s house. I checked in with my therapist every night, saw my psychiatrist once a week. With all those measures in place, I was safer than I would have been had I been on my own. Safer, but still wanting to die. I would find a way, eventually, to make it happen. Overdose on Benadryl, perhaps. Walk to the beauty supply and buy those sharp little eyebrow-trimming scissors. Already, I’d lost so much of myself to depression dulling my senses, replacing my personality with anhedonia. I’d think about my family. Especially my six-year-old nephew and my dog. My brother and sister-in-law just had to explain to my nephew what happened to Pop Pop, my dad who passed away less than a year earlier. And my dog? If we were alone when I went through with it, she, after, would be alone and confused. What would happen to her if EMTs or the police, and not my mom or a friend, got to her first? I hesitated. Torn between guilt and my suicidal urge, I thought I at least had to consider what I deemed my last resort. Desperate for something other than the life I was living—not much more than insomnia or somnolence, being bed-bound or pacing, occasionally taking the dog outside or sitting on my best friend’s stoop—I made an appointment with a psychiatrist, Dr. Woodson, who performed ECT, to see if I was a good candidate. He said I was. I’m pretty sure no one truly knows how electroconvulsive therapy works, but people swear by it. Patients, doctors, scientists. Possibly, the seizure helps release neurotransmitters which alter brain chemistry, relieving symptoms of depression. Or, the seizure permanently changes neural pathways. Before my appointment with Dr. Woodson, I skimmed a memoir where the author described how their depression, after ECT, had completely disappeared. I got most of my information from the ECT scenes in One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest and Requiem for a Dream , where Jack Nicholson’s Randle and Ellen Burstyn’s Sara absorb the electricity and seize without general anesthesia. I knew enough to know the use of general anesthesia was standard now and had been since the 1960s. And I did know about the procedure’s potential problems, too. But the side effects , Mom said. Dr. Woodson clearly laid out what he called slight possibilities for memory loss and cognitive impairment. He said the memory loss usually was contained to the time during which you received the treatment. Those memories will likely come back , he assured me. Slight. Usually . Likely . Already, I’d lost so much of myself to depression dulling my senses, replacing my personality with anhedonia. Other than the desire to kill myself, I had no real desires, no strong opinions. I felt as if I had nothing to look forward to. I hardly had the energy to think. Impaired cognition wouldn’t be unfamiliar. At this point I couldn’t work. What started as an illness morphed into disability. Black, female, and disabled: a minority three times over which likely wouldn’t help me find any sense of autonomy amidst my ailing confidence. I thought: Could things really get much worse? I’d already left the Erica I knew behind years ago when the severe depression settled in. Now I faced the hardest decision I’d ever make. Maybe lose even more of who I was but possibly have a chance at survival or, sooner than later, at my own hand, die . I scheduled my first ECT treatment for Monday, April 4, 2022. I can’t remember the specific consent documents, but I’ve looked at several examples online, all basically the same. Confusion can result but generally clears in an hour. Retrograde memory loss sometimes goes back one, two, or more years. For a brief period, difficulty with aspects of learning and thinking, in addition to anterograde amnesia (making new memories) can happen. The risk of death is very low. And there’s always something like this: Reports show some people have memory problems and cognitive impairment much more serious and long-lasting. Not enough research exists to predict which patients will have major debilitation. I was sick but I was a competent adult. I could sign the consent form and I did. items.title: Exclusive Cover Reveal of SHAMEWRECK by Peggy Shinner
items.summary: Electric Literature is pleased to reveal the cover of Shamewreck by Peggy Shinner, which will be published on February 9, 2027 by Mad Creek Books. You can pre-order your copy here . For readers of Eula Biss and Cathy Park Hong, essays that knit cultural criticism, social history, and personal experience to excavate the entanglements of shame, power, language, and identity. In Shamewreck , Peggy Shinner interrogates the entanglement of shame and language, casting shame as a moral force, a conscience-beast, an umpire, the fellow who awaits when you come home. These essays grapple with the nuclear bombing of Bikini Atoll and the emergence, four days later, of the bikini in Paris; the link between property and personhood and what it means to die without possessions; the mutability of language and how shamefaced once meant “modest and bashful,” before morphing into the opposite, “abashed and ashamed”; how talkative women were thought to be sloppy women, like Eve (loose of mouth and morals); how occupation once meant “heterosexual intercourse” and now means “military invasion.” Parsing the dark undercurrents of popular culture alongside her own experiences as a queer woman, Shinner exhorts us to abandon willful unseeing and consider the legacies of language. Take a look, she urges, you can buy a new car in 21st century America and for your money get two masters and a slave key. Shamewreck complicates our notions of shame and shamelessness and rescues them from the refuse pile, reclaiming shame as a potent moral adjudicator. Here is the cover, designed by Charles Brock: Peggy Shinner: Shamewreck is, in many ways, an invitation to look at the unsightly or, to put it another way, the unseen, and make it visible. What would such a book look like? There were three elements I was sure of: strong type, saturated color, and no human figures. I wanted to steer clear of the tired visual tropes of shame: head bowed, shoulders slumped, gaze averted. So I had a feel for the cover, but not a specific image. At the last minute I sent my editor a photo of a bombed US naval ship at Bikini Atoll, referencing one of the essays in the book. An actual, irradiated shipwreck. Then the prestidigitation, out of sight, out of my sight, happened. Soon the cover arrived. Not the ship I sent but another ship, on its side, mostly submerged, nose up and precariously tilted, heading toward the bottom, completely unanchored. Then and now I was astounded. I love the cover for its somewhat queasy green color (shame can be queasy-making); the visual and aural rhyming of shipwreck/shamewreck, both ship and shame upended; the water, too, upended, along the whole length of the spine; the horizontal bands of deep purple, the encapsulated lowercase typography in an astonishing pink, an explosion of color and the centerpiece, pinning it all down. The whole disturbing disturbance. I’m grateful to Charles Brock for his vision and his palette and how the cover surprises me every time I look at it. Charles Brock: A shipwreck was suggested as a possible image for the cover. There was concern that the cover might look like a history book with a ship on the cover. So the choice was made to rotate the image and use a halftone effect so that it had more of a graphic feel as opposed to a photo. The author likes strong type. I took Barbara Kruger as inspiration and used Futura Bold Oblique for the cover type. I think the graphic treatment on the image, combined with the bold type and unconventional colors work well to communicate that Shamewreck is not a history book.
